title: Prediction Markets Aren't Casinos, but 90% of the Volume Is Sports
dek: Kalshi traded four years of compliance for 90% market share, but its revenue structure looks more like a bookmaker's; what's genuinely underrated are the quiet markets like FDA approvals.
why: The first half is founder narrative; the value is in the middle and back: how contracts are written, sports at 90%, regulatory risk. Worth listening for anyone who wants to understand the mechanics of prediction markets.
who: Founders and investors interested in prediction markets, regulatory arbitrage and information aggregation mechanisms; anyone who wants to understand Kalshi's business model and compliance path.
skip: The opening history — Greek oracles, Andean potato farmers and the Iowa Electronic Markets — can be fast-forwarded.

points.h: Comply for four years first, then open your first market
points.body: Kalshi's two founders wrote "regulatory first" into the company's principles and spent four years getting regulatory approval before launching their first market. Mansoor says this is anti-Silicon Valley: everyone else builds the product and patches in compliance later, while they went to the federal government first and asked, "how should this be regulated?" The cost was that for the first four years he wanted to quit almost every day, held up by "the cost of regret is too high." The payoff: in 2024 a federal appeals court ruled Kalshi could list election contracts, landing before the presidential election. Mansoor attributes the 90% market share directly to that path: institutions would rather plug into a platform inside the system, because changing the rules from outside the system is harder.

points.h: Prediction markets force you to shut up, not to take a position
points.body: Robin Hanson lays out three mechanisms that make prediction markets more accurate than polls or expert interviews. First, people being interviewed have an incentive to be interesting, dramatic and to please the questioner, while the market only rewards being right. Second, the market gives you an incentive to shut up about topics you don't understand — you only bet in the few markets where you genuinely have an edge, whereas interviewees will answer confidently on things they don't know. Third, the market doesn't require you to have a direct opinion on a topic; it invites you to find the biases and errors in other people's pricing, and pays you to correct them. He closes with the old poker-table line: sit down and look for the sucker; if you can't find him, you're the sucker — so don't play that market.

points.h: Internal prediction markets die on the project owner's excuse
points.body: Eli Lilly ran an internal prediction market in the early 2000s that successfully predicted which drug compounds would pass Phase III trials; Google ran one called Google Profit. Both were considered effective, and neither survived. Hanson's explanation: the project owner wants to know whether they'll deliver on time, but wants even more a good excuse if they fail. And the most useful excuse is precisely "everything was going fine, and then at the last minute something nobody could have foreseen happened." A market that keeps accurately predicting "will you be late" invalidates that excuse in advance, so nobody wants it to exist.

points.h: Domain expertise is not the key skill for forecasting the future
points.body: Mansoor cites Philip Tetlock's Superforecasting research: put experts in a given domain — geopolitics, say — up against a group of non-experts forecasting the same set of events, and the non-experts win. His explanation is that domain experts become too doctrinaire over time, while people who can step back and look at things coolly are better calibrated and less biased. Mansoor says this is a fairly heretical claim in politics, academia and financial analysis circles — it means that if you want a more accurate answer, you should look for a diverse group of participants who pride themselves on self-calibration, critical reading and filtering information, not an authority in some field. He treats this as Kalshi's underlying logic.

points.h: One contract takes a month to write, for grammar and apostrophes
points.body: Nicole Kagan writes the contracts and self-certifies them with the CFTC. The most complex category is "what someone will say in a given speech," and they recently rewrote the rules because a pile of grammar questions came up: what if there's an apostrophe? If they misspeak or mispronounce it, does it still count as the same word? What if it appears inside a proper noun? What if the livestream cuts out midway and it's uploaded somewhere else later? Those rules took over a month to write, seven or eight pages, extremely detailed. When Bloomberg reported on it, they guessed the rules were for automated processing and must be for AI; Kagan says not at all — they were written so users could understand them, and they never considered that "what a human can understand, a computer can probably understand too."

points.h: When you can't call a winner, settle at the last fair price
points.body: Kalshi's contracts are usually binary: pay $1 if the event happens, $0 if it doesn't, with every position fully collateralized — if one side bets 30 cents, someone must bet 70. But some situations can't be judged yes or no. Cardi B was clearly dancing in her seven-second Super Bowl halftime cameo, but had no mic, so it couldn't be confirmed whether she was singing; the team said "we are epistemically uncertain" and settled at the last fair price. Another case is 50-50: when multiple people win simultaneously, each settles at 50 cents. Kagan says they have the right to do this when whether an event meets the criteria is "genuinely unclear," and they've already revised the halftime contract — the new rules require an audible lead or backing vocal, and under the new rules Cardi B didn't perform.

points.h: Ninety percent of volume comes from sports, and that's the most uncomfortable fact
points.body: Dubner puts it directly: roughly 90% of Kalshi's volume is concentrated in a category barely mentioned until then — sports, the business that makes DraftKings and FanDuel nervous. Mansoor's response is that sports' share is falling fast and other categories are growing faster, but he concedes "10% is also a lot, don't forget we're big." He insists on distinguishing gambling from trading: all derivatives markets are mostly speculative, speculation provides liquidity, and the key isn't whether there's speculation but the business model — one model hunts for losers and bans winners, the other pursues price discovery and wants smart people in. He also concedes the second model carries risk, saying there is "responsible gambling" and "responsible trading," and platforms have a responsibility to monitor.

points.h: Seventy to eighty percent of active users never place an order
points.body: Mansoor says one of his favorite numbers is that 70% to 80% of active users don't trade — they just log in every day, keep it next to X and a few newspapers, and use it to calibrate or check information. Kalshi's business model is a neutral platform, like the NYSE or Nasdaq, taking an average 1% on trades and not caring who wins or loses. He also says the information environment is getting more polarized and the signal-to-noise ratio is falling, because social media algorithms reward clickbait: write a nuanced, restrained, multi-paragraph take on X and you get four likes; write something extreme and absurd and you get tens of thousands. Prediction markets have exactly the opposite incentive — the nuanced, boring, well-calibrated judgment is the one that makes money.
